model:claude|title:discovering and explo.content_excerpt: Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities. We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure , which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory. After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction: We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and patched as of Chrome 156 , with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer. The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined. Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly. That fix is available to users. After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that let an attacker extract photos and other personal information from a stolen Android phone without unlocking it. The work combined three methods: source code analysis of the open-source parts of Android, reverse engineering and deobfuscation of the Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a physical Google Pixel 9. model:deepseek|title:deepseek releases a.content_excerpt: Research prototype for reference only, not an official DeepSeek product. This code grew out of our team's day-to-day development work, with much of the engineering done by coding agents. Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Review and adapt it before using it in your own environment. We have adapted it for publication, so it is not identical to our internal version or the implementation described in Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype. dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person. It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. docs/000-philosophy.md explains the principle and what it asks of the operator. It asks one short question at a time, shows the full plan once, and then installs and configures everything. SETUP.md is what it follows.

model:deepseek|ver:4.1|variant:flash|tit.content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9× our single-node result from the first post and $38.96 per GPU-hour at DeepSeek's off-peak prices. A specialized decode path reaches 826 tokens/s for a single user. Against DeepInfer, DeepSeek's own engine, vLLM's decode throughput is within 6% across batch sizes 8–256, and its prefill tracks DeepInfer's published curve. The efficiency comes from deliberate engineering on components that vLLM already has, built on the kernels DeepSeek open-sourced. This post walks through our performance study, breaks down each optimization, and shares the lessons we learned: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72: vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP (gold) achieves a further 7.9× throughput increase over our aggregated single-node result from the first post . Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( source ). DeepInfer is DeepSeek's own inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released this week as an offline engine with published prefill and decode curves. It is the most relevant reference for this model, so before going into our optimizations we show where vLLM stands against it. Decode. Under DeepSeek's decode configuration (131K context, nextn=3), vLLM on GB200 achieves throughput within 6% of DeepInfer's published results across batch sizes 8 to 256 (Figure 2). Figure 2: Decode output throughput per GPU vs. batch size at 131K context, nextn=3. vLLM on GB200 vs. DeepInfer's published results, read from the charts in its README ( source ). Prefill. DeepInfer's published prefill curve uses EP4DP4 with 32 redundant experts and a 140-token bounded replay, on hardware the chart does not state, and we read its values off the chart. Our run uses DEP2 on GB300 with no redundant experts, a 128-token replay and our own prompts. Because the setups differ, we do not read the gap between the two curves as an engine-to-engine speedup. What Figure 3 shows is that vLLM's DEP2 prefill tracks DeepSeek's own engine across the range they published. Figure 3: Prefill throughput vs. new tokens. vLLM DEP2 on GB300 vs. DeepInfer's published curve (EP4DP4, 32 redundant experts, 140-token replay, hardware not stated), read from the chart in its README ( source ). model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . story|title:how ai agents shape experts.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. story|ver:4.1|title:granite switch 4 1 1.content_excerpt: Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.
